newsitem.title: USA: Worldcom's UUNET tightens Internet rules.
newsitem.headline: Worldcom's UUNET tightens Internet rules.

text.p: UUNET Technologies Inc, a unit of WorldCom Inc, said Monday it would no longer accept Internet routing requests from Internet Service Providers (ISPs) that have insufficent network infrastructure to handle reciprocal amounts of traffic from UUNET.
UUNET, a leading Internet Service Provider (ISP) to businesses, said it would continue to peer with ISP's that can route traffic "on a bilateral and equitable basis."
The company said change was necessary because of the radical changes in economics that have occurred in the Internet transmission business in the past few years.
Peering refers to the tradition of free passage of Internet message traffic over the various networks which collectively combine to form the public Internet.

Such free passage, begun in the days when government and university research organizations were the dominant funders of the Internet, was a key impetus to the creation of the Internet as a open communications medium.
But it has proved increasingly unwieldy in recent years as Internet traffic volumes have surged and commercial service providers have stepped into provide much of the network infrastructure.
UUNET's plans, which have been widely reported in the coputer industry trade press, have stirred an outcry among some smaller Internet Service Providers.
Industry analysts believe UUNET's move is likely to accelerate the increasing consolidation of the ISP business.

"A few years ago all ISPs were generally the same size and used each other's infrastructures to a more or less equal extent," John Sidgmore, UUNET's president and chief executive said. "Today that situation no longer exists and consequently there are many cases where peering is not appropriate."
UUNET said it has received numerous peering requests from small regional ISP's and companies which provide what are known in the industry as "web server farm" services.

Web server farms typically are run by Internet Service Providers who operate a network of computers used to host customer web sites. Server farms usually do not own backbone tranmission equipment in contrast to companies like UUNET.

UUNET said server farm peering requests are, in effect, demands to provide national and international data transport and other services to companies which do not have the capacity to provide similar services in return.
Companies requesting peering in these situations use UUNET's network for free, after UUNET has spent hundreds of millions of dollars to create its infrastructure, it said.
"This is a purely economic decision," Sidgmore said, adding that, "We are 100 percent in favor of interconnection and won't deny access to anyone."
"However where the use of our respective infrastructures would clearly be imbalanced, we cannot reasonably be expected to provide our transport, route management and support resources at no charge."

For those ISP's, or web server farms, seeking transport and route management services from UUNET, but which do not qualify as peers, UUNET said it offers wholesale connection services beginning at monthly rates of $2,000 for T1 connections and $6,000 for fractional T3 connections.
T1 lines are high-speed lines that carry voice and data traffic at 1.54 megabits per second. Fractional T3 lines can carry traffic at variable speeds up to 45 megabits per second.
UUNET currently provides such wholesale connections to several hundred Internet Service Providers.

UUNET's network consists of a global backbone with multiple DS-3 links carry traffic at 45 million bit per second on all major routes providing a total capacity well in excess of five gigabits, or billions of bits, per second.

UUNET said a major principle of its policy is to peer with ISP's that operate a national network based on a high-speed DS-3 (or faster) backbone and which connect to UUNET at DS-3 or greater speeds in at least four geographically diverse locations.
(( -- Eric Auchard, New York newsdesk, 212-859-1736 ))
